source.text: Ὅτε οὖν ἠρίστησαν λέγει τῷ Σίμωνι Πέτρῳ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Σίμων ⸀Ἰωάννου, ἀγαπᾷς με πλέον τούτων; λέγει αὐτῷ· Ναί, κύριε, σὺ οἶδας ὅτι φιλῶ σε. λέγει αὐτῷ· Βόσκε τὰ ἀρνία μου.

translation.text: So when they had eaten breakfast[a], Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him[b], “Feed my lambs.”

footnotes.text: Greek has two different verbs here: Jesus asks with ἀγαπάω ('love'), and Peter replies with φιλέω ('love, have affection for'). Many interpreters see a distinction; others take the variation as stylistic. The main text renders both as 'love' to avoid overstating a contrast the context does not make explicit.
'More than these' may mean 'more than these men do' or 'more than these things.' The Greek leaves the comparison implicit.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb ἀριστάω refers specifically to taking the morning meal. 'Had eaten breakfast' preserves the temporal sense naturally in English and avoids the overly bare 'had eaten.'
Although the Greek uses the historical present, standard English narrative style normally renders it with a past tense. 'Said' communicates the discourse clearly without awkwardness.

The genitive Ἰωάννου is most naturally rendered as a patronymic, 'son of John.' This follows the direct Greek reading here. 'Son of Jonah' reflects a different traditional form known from Matt 16:17, not this verse's wording.
The ordinary and most natural rendering of ἀγαπάω is 'love.' The verse's rhetorical force depends on the direct personal question, and English should preserve that simplicity.

alternatives: more than you love these things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek expression is elliptical and genuinely ambiguous: it may compare Peter's love for Jesus with his attachment to the other disciples or to the surrounding things, or compare Peter's love with that of the others. The traditional and concise 'more than these' best preserves the ambiguity rather than resolving it.
Per doctrine defaults, κύριος is rendered 'Lord.' In Johannine context, Peter addresses Jesus with reverence that exceeds a merely polite 'sir.'
'You know' is the direct and idiomatic rendering of οἶδα here, fitting Peter's appeal to Jesus' personal knowledge.

Although φιλέω can emphasize affection or friendship, in this context 'I love' is the most natural English equivalent. Rendering it differently in the main text would overstate a lexical distinction that is debated and may not be semantically sharp in Johannine usage; the distinction is better preserved in a footnote.
βόσκω specifically denotes feeding rather than the broader shepherding sense. 'Feed' best matches the imperative and prepares for the later alternation with ποιμαίνω in the passage.
ἀρνίον denotes a lamb or young sheep. 'Lambs' is clear, natural, and preserves the pastoral imagery without unnecessary diminutive wording.
The possessive pronoun marks Jesus' ownership and care over the flock. The simple possessive 'my' preserves this directly.

source.text: λέγει αὐτῷ πάλιν δεύτερον· Σίμων ⸀Ἰωάννου, ἀγαπᾷς με; λέγει αὐτῷ· Ναί, κύριε, σὺ οἶδας ὅτι φιλῶ σε. λέγει αὐτῷ· Ποίμαινε τὰ πρόβατά μου.

translation.text: He said to him again a second time[a], “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him[b], “Shepherd my sheep.”

footnotes.text: Greek uses two different verbs for 'love' in this exchange: Jesus asks with agapaō, and Peter replies with phileō. Many interpreters see a distinction; others see stylistic variation. The main text renders both as 'love' to avoid overstating the difference.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The combination of πάλιν and δεύτερον explicitly marks repetition. Rendering both elements preserves the Greek emphasis rather than collapsing them into a single adverb.
The genitive Ἰωάννου is naturally rendered as a patronymic, 'son of John.' 'Son of Jonah' reflects a different traditional form from Matt 16:17, not this Greek reading.

ἀγαπάω is best rendered with the ordinary English verb 'love.' This keeps the lexical connection with Peter’s reply while avoiding overinterpretation of a supposed sharp distinction between ἀγαπάω and φιλέω in this context.
Direct object pronoun retained straightforwardly.
A simple affirmative best matches the discourse tone.
Per doctrine defaults, κύριος is rendered 'Lord.' In Johannine context Peter addresses Jesus with reverential recognition, so 'Lord' is preferable to the merely polite 'sir.'
The explicit pronoun adds mild emphasis, but standard English can convey this naturally without overloading the line. The sense is preserved in 'you know.'

alternatives: that I am fond of you
that I have affection for you
lexical_decisions.rationale: φιλέω here is also best rendered 'love' in idiomatic English. Rendering it differently from ἀγαπάω in the main text would imply a lexical contrast stronger than the context clearly demands; the variation is better noted in a footnote.
ποιμαίνω denotes the activity of a shepherd—guiding, caring for, and overseeing the flock. 'Shepherd' preserves the pastoral metaphor more fully than the narrower 'feed' or the vaguer 'tend.'
πρόβατα literally means sheep. 'My sheep' preserves the concrete pastoral image and the possessive relation to Jesus.

source.text: λέγει αὐτῷ τὸ τρίτον· Σίμων ⸀Ἰωάννου, φιλεῖς με; ἐλυπήθη ὁ Πέτρος ὅτι εἶπεν αὐτῷ τὸ τρίτον· Φιλεῖς με; καὶ ⸀εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Κύριε, ⸂πάντα σὺ⸃ οἶδας, σὺ γινώσκεις ὅτι φιλῶ σε. λέγει αὐτῷ ⸀ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Βόσκε τὰ ⸀πρόβατά μου.

translation.text: He said to him the third time[a], “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, “Do you love me?” And he said to him, “Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you.” Jesus said to him[b], “Feed my sheep.”

footnotes.text: The Greek uses φιλέω here ('love, have affection for') where earlier in the exchange Jesus had used ἀγαπάω in two questions. Some interpreters see a meaningful distinction; others regard the verbs as overlapping in this context. The translation preserves the exchange with 'love' and does not force a sharper contrast than the Greek clearly requires.

Greek uses two verbs for 'know' in Peter's reply: οἶδα and γινώσκω. English normally renders both as 'know' here; the repetition may suggest nuance, but not one that can be expressed naturally without over-interpretation.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Idiomatic temporal accusative; 'the third time' is natural English and preserves the repeated questioning motif.
The genitive Ἰωάννου is most naturally patronymic, hence 'son of John.' 'Son of Jonah' reflects a different traditional form from other passages, not this Greek reading.

φιλέω commonly denotes love/affection. In English, 'love' best preserves the solemn relational force of the exchange. Although some interpreters distinguish φιλέω from ἀγαπάω in this context, the difference is debated and should not be overstated in translation; the lexical variation is better noted in a footnote than encoded as different English verbs.
The passive conveys Peter's sorrow/distress. 'Was grieved' is both natural and weightier than 'was saddened,' fitting the emotional force of the scene.
Per doctrine default for κύριος, 'Lord' is preferred. In Johannine context and in Peter's address to the risen Jesus, this carries more than mere politeness.
'All things' preserves the breadth and solemnity of πάντα while remaining clear in English. The fronted σὺ is reflected by explicit 'you' without awkward inversion.

Both verbs concern knowing, though with different nuances. English normally uses 'know' for both here; forcing a distinction would over-interpret the contrast. The repetition is preserved, and the possible nuance is noted in a footnote.
βόσκω specifically means to feed/provide pasture, distinct from ποιμαίνω ('shepherd/tend'). 'Feed' preserves that specificity.
πρόβατα are sheep, not specifically lambs (contrast ἀρνία in v. 15). 'Sheep' preserves the lexical distinction across the passage.
